edition: Newton, Principia, Andrew Motte trans., 1729 (Wikisource); Book I, Section I, Lemma VI; Plate 2, Fig. 1.

figures.caption: As a point B on a curve approaches the point of contact A, the angle between the chord AB and the tangent AD is diminished without limit and ultimately vanishes.

text.latex: Here is \textcolor{arcblue}{the arc $ACB$}, a piece of curve fixed in position, rising from the point of contact $A$ up through $C$ to a nearby point $B$. The phrase \emph{continuous curvature} means the curve bends \emph{smoothly} — at every point, including $A$, it has one definite direction and no sharp corner. This smoothness is Newton's standing assumption, the supposition he will not let go of. \textcolor{arcblue}{This arc} is the object whose ultimate behaviour near $A$ we mean to investigate.

Now join $A$ to $B$ by \textcolor{chordgreen}{the straight chord $AB$}, a shortcut that cuts beneath \textcolor{arcblue}{the arc}. Imagine the point $B$ now sliding down \textcolor{arcblue}{the curve} toward $A$. As $B$ draws nearer, \textcolor{chordgreen}{the chord $AB$} grows shorter and shorter, and its direction settles into the direction of the curve at $A$. It is this swivelling of \textcolor{chordgreen}{the chord} that the next step compares against the tangent.

Draw \textcolor{tanorange}{the tangent $AD$}, the straight line that just grazes \textcolor{arcblue}{the curve} at $A$, matching its direction there and extending both ways. Between \textcolor{tanorange}{the tangent} and \textcolor{chordgreen}{the chord} opens \textcolor{anglered}{the angle $BAD$}. As $B$ approaches $A$, \textcolor{chordgreen}{the chord} swivels toward \textcolor{tanorange}{the tangent}, and \textcolor{anglered}{this angle} is diminished \emph{in infinitum}. For if \textcolor{anglered}{the angle} did \emph{not} vanish, \textcolor{arcblue}{the arc} would meet \textcolor{tanorange}{the tangent} at a finite rectilinear angle — a sharp elbow at $A$ — and the curvature there would not be continuous, against the supposition. Hence ultimately $\angle BAD \to 0$. \textit{Q.E.D.}
